hook.support: Two phone plans. One says $25 a month. One says $35. Easy, right? But one has a catch. You only see it if you read the papers side by side.
hook.core: Two phone plans: $25 a month or $35 a month. Easy choice? Not if the cheap one locks you in for two years and charges for every extra gig. The information is all there in the documents. The skill is reading two of them side by side, fairly, and judging which one tells you the truth most clearly.
hook.extend: Banks, phone companies, power companies and landlords all publish documents that do the same job: describe an offer. Some make the important details easy to find. Others bury them. Comparing documents with the same purpose, and judging how well each informs you, is how you choose well and spot what’s hidden.

why.support: Comparing deals saves you money. It also shows you which company is honest.
why.core: Comparing properly can save you hundreds of dollars a year on phones, power and banking. It also teaches you which companies make information easy to find, and which hide it.
why.extend: Choosing between similar offers is a constant adult task. Judging documents side by side, on the same criteria, protects your money. It also shows you which companies talk to you honestly.

articles.title: Apples with apples

body.support:
Phone plans, bank accounts and power deals all come with papers. The papers tell you about the deal.

Here is how to compare two deals:

1. **Same kind of deal.** Compare two phone plans. Not a phone plan and a bank account.
2. **Same things.** Check the cost, what you get, and the catch, for both.
3. **Cost per year.** Add up every fee for 12 months.
4. **Which paper is clearer?** Can you find the cost fast? Or is it hidden?
.
Phone and internet plans must have a **Critical Information Summary**. It’s a short sheet with the key facts.

Comparison websites can help. But some earn money from the deals they show. The government has free ones too, like **Victorian Energy Compare** for power.
body.core:
Phone plans, bank accounts, power deals and rentals all come with documents that describe the offer. Comparing them well can save you hundreds of dollars a year.

**1. Compare like with like.** Two phone plans with similar data. Two everyday bank accounts. Comparing different kinds of deal tells you nothing.

**2. Use the same criteria for both.** Decide what matters before you start. Usually:
- **total cost** (including every fee).
- **what’s included** (data, features, interest).
- **the catch** (contract length, exit fees, price rises, extra charges).

**3. Work out the cost per year.** Monthly prices hide yearly totals. Add every fee for 12 months.

**4. Judge the documents, not just the deals.** Which one puts the important facts up front? Which uses plain language? Which hides the catch in small print? A company that explains clearly is often easier to deal with later.

**Useful documents:** phone and internet companies must give you a **Critical Information Summary** for each plan: a short sheet with the minimum cost, inclusions and key conditions. Banks publish fee pages and terms.

**Comparison sites** can save time, but check who runs them. Some earn a **commission** from the deals they list, and may not include every company. Government sites, like **Victorian Energy Compare**, are free and independent.
body.extend:
Banks, telcos, energy retailers and landlords all publish documents with the same basic purpose: to describe an offer. Comparing them well is a skill in reading, not just maths.

**1. Compare texts with the same purpose.** Two plans of the same type and similar size; two everyday accounts. Otherwise the comparison is meaningless.

**2. Set criteria first, and apply them equally.** Typically: **total cost** (all fees), **inclusions**, and **conditions** (contract length, exit fees, price changes, excess charges). Deciding criteria first stops a flashy feature from distracting you.

**3. Standardise the numbers.** Convert to a yearly cost, including one-off and conditional fees.

**4. Evaluate how effectively each document informs.** Are key facts prominent or buried? Is the language plain or technical? Are the conditions near the price, or pages away? Effectiveness is part of the comparison: opaque documents carry risk.

Standardised documents help. Telcos must provide a **Critical Information Summary** for each plan, so the same facts appear in the same places.

Be critical of **comparison sites**. In 2014 the ACCC found that some didn’t make clear how much of the market they covered, or that commercial deals could shape what they showed. Independent government tools, such as **Victorian Energy Compare**, avoid that conflict.

caseStudies.title: Who’s doing the comparing?

body.support:
Comparison websites show you lots of deals at once. They are popular.

In **2014**, the **ACCC** looked at these sites. The ACCC is the government group that protects shoppers.

It found some sites did not tell people:
- that they did **not** show every company.
- that some companies **paid** them.

That could push people to a deal that cost more.

The ACCC told the sites to be clearer. It also told shoppers to check who runs the site.
body.core:
Comparison websites promise to find you the best deal on phones, power or health insurance in seconds. Millions of Australians use them.

In **2014**, the **ACCC**, the government group that protects shoppers, wrote a report on comparison sites. It looked at sites that compare power, phone and internet, and health insurance.

The ACCC was worried about two things:
- Some sites didn’t make clear that they **didn’t show every company**.
- Some had **money deals** with the companies they listed, and people didn’t know. These deals could push people to dearer products, even when cheaper ones existed.
.
In 2015, the ACCC wrote guides for comparison sites and for shoppers. Its advice: check who runs the site, how it makes money, and whether it shows every company.
body.extend:
Comparison websites present themselves as neutral guides to the cheapest phone plan, power deal or health insurance.

In **2014**, after complaints, the **ACCC** published a report on comparison websites. It looked at sites comparing power, phone and internet plans, and health insurance.

The ACCC identified two key concerns:
- Sites weren’t always clear about **market coverage**: how many companies they actually compared.
- Some had **hidden money deals** with the companies they listed. These could steer people to dearer products when cheaper ones existed.
.
In 2015, the ACCC published guides for comparison sites and for shoppers.

The lesson is to treat the comparison itself as a text to judge. A ranking is only as trustworthy as whoever made it. Ask who made it, how they’re paid, and what they left out. Then check the original documents yourself.

teacher.overview: The boss course for Real-World Docs. Students compare two real documents with the same purpose (phone plans’ Critical Information Summaries, bank account fee pages, energy offers) on set criteria, standardise costs per year, identify the catch, and evaluate how effectively each document informs, then write a recommendation. The case study is the ACCC’s 2014 report on comparison websites (market coverage and undisclosed commercial relationships).
prep: Bookmark Critical Information Summaries for two or three real phone plans, and Victorian Energy Compare, for students who need a starting point.
Check the ACCC page is reachable.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 plan type (month-to-month, 40 GB); 2 minimum monthly charge; 3 minimum total cost (one month, no lock-in); 4 excess data (slowed, not charged); 5 exclusions/extra charges (international); 6 exit (no fee).

**Quiz yearly cost:** Plan A $35 × 12 = $420; Plan B $33 × 12 = $396.

**Sort:** similar phone plans — fair; ignoring a fee — not fair; two everyday accounts — fair; data vs interest — not fair; two yearly power costs — fair; site that only lists paying companies — not fair.

**Case study:** lack of transparency about market coverage, and undisclosed commercial relationships that could steer people to dearer products; check who runs the site, how it earns money and how much of the market it covers.
realityCheck: **Finding the official documents is half the skill.** Some students will default to ads. Model searching for “[plan name] critical information summary”.
**Yearly cost maths trips students up.** Have calculators ready, and check one example together.
**Avoid recommending real companies yourself.** The decision is the student’s reasoning; keep the class discussion about documents, not brands.
**Energy offers are complicated.** Victorian Energy Compare simplifies them; recommend it for students choosing power.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students enjoy “catching out” confusing documents, and some take their findings home.

levels.core: Aimed at about Years 5–6 reading: the standard version with criteria, yearly costs, the CIS, the ACCC case and a recommendation.
levels.extend: Aimed at about Year 7 and up: evaluating effectiveness, market coverage and commissions, and testing a comparison site.
